title: Where do you meet patterns in nature and at school?
description: Day and night come back in turn, and the school timetable repeats every week. The video shows that each repeats by a rule, and Keeko's doubt, that a pattern must be a list of numbers, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: anything that repeats by a rule is a pattern, with or without numbers. Watch for students who think a pattern must be a list of numbers.

source: Name two patterns you meet in a day, one in nature and one a
video_script.why: The child sees that a pattern is anything that repeats by a rule, in nature or at school, and not only a list of numbers.
video_script.substitution: A pattern is something that repeats or grows by a rule.
video_script.anchor: the Sun and Moon in the sky and a school timetable, the two patterns of one day
video_script.wrong_answer: a pattern is only a list of numbers
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says a pattern is only a list of numbers, so the Sun cannot be one. Day and night come back in order without any number, so the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Day and night, and the weekly timetable, are patterns

final_answer.value: day and night; the weekly timetable
final_answer.spoken: day and night in nature, and the weekly timetable at school

hold_back: Day and night, and the weekly timetable, are patterns
never_show: a pattern is only a list of numbers
maths_rules: nature: day follows night and night follows day, in the same order every time
school: the bell rings at fixed times and the timetable repeats every week
both repeat by a rule, so both are patterns
slip: no number is needed for something to repeat by a rule
video_script.design: One idea: a pattern is anything that repeats by a rule. Assumes nothing. Wrong idea: patterns are only lists of numbers. The two examples stay on the board to the end.
